pages.text: Out in the schoolyard, the teacher drew a big yellow chalk circle on the ground surrounded by wider rings. “This centre circle is the Sun,” she said. “Tanko, you will play the Sun today. And remember, everyone: never look straight at the real Sun in the sky, because it can harm your eyes.”

“This centre circle is the Sun,” she said.
“Tanko, you will play the Sun today.
And remember, everyone: never look straight at the real Sun in the sky, because it can harm your eyes.”
pages.alt: In a sunlit Ghanaian schoolyard, Tanko wearing a yellow paper sun crown stands in a central chalk circle while his teacher and classmates gather.

pages.text: “There are eight planets in our solar system,” said the teacher. “Each one moves around the Sun along a curved path called an orbit.” Nikoi played Earth and walked slowly around Tanko, while other children walked in bigger circles further out.
sentences: “There are eight planets in our solar system,” said the teacher.
“Each one moves around the Sun along a curved path called an orbit.” Nikoi played Earth and walked slowly around Tanko, while other children walked in bigger circles further out.
pages.alt: Nikoi holds a blue-and-green clay ball as she walks along a chalk ring around Tanko while classmates holding clay planets walk on wider outer rings.

pages.text: “Earth is the planet where we live,” said Nikoi. “It has air and liquid water.” Another classmate walked in a small circle right around Nikoi, holding a grey clay ball. “I am the Moon!” she said. The teacher explained, “A satellite is a body that goes around a planet. The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite.”

The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite.”
pages.alt: A smiling girl holding a grey clay Moon walks in a small circle around Nikoi holding the blue-and-green clay Earth while Tanko watches from the centre.

pages.text: “The Sun is a star,” said the teacher. “It is a giant ball of hot glowing gas, much bigger than all the planets put together. Its strong pull keeps the planets moving around it. That is why the Sun is at the centre of the solar system.” Tanko stood very tall. “I hold the whole family together!” he grinned, and the class laughed.

pages.alt: Tanko stands tall and smiling in the central chalk circle as his laughing classmates walk along concentric chalk orbits around him.

pages.text: “What benefits does the Sun give us on Earth?” asked the teacher. “Light and heat!” answered the class. “Sunlight helps green plants make food and dries our washed clothes,” added Nikoi. “And it warms water on Earth so vapour rises to form rain clouds.”

“And it warms water on Earth so vapour rises to form rain clouds.”
pages.alt: In the bright schoolyard, Nikoi gestures toward green garden leaves, colourful cloths drying on a line, and white clouds under the warm sky.

pages.text: Back in class, the children painted the solar system and moulded clay planets around a yellow clay Sun at the centre. “A planet is not a star,” said Tanko. “Planets shine because they reflect the Sun’s light, not their own.” Nikoi nodded. “Every orbit keeps the solar system moving smoothly.”

activities.question: What sits at the centre of our solar system?
What is the Moon to planet Earth?

activities.prompt: Put the solar-system lesson in order.
items: Tanko stands in the middle as the Sun.
Nikoi walks around Tanko as Earth.
A classmate circles Nikoi as the Moon.
The class moulds clay planets indoors.

activities.definition: The curved path a planet takes as it travels around the Sun.
distractors: A hot ball of glowing gas
A cloud of rain in the sky

glossary.definition: Large round bodies in space that move in orbits around a star such as the Sun.
The curved path a planet or moon follows around a larger body in space.
A body in space that travels around a planet; the Moon is Earth’s natural satellite.
A huge ball of hot glowing gas in space that produces its own light and heat.
